Abraham Lincoln's first inauguration. On March 4, 1861, Abraham Lincoln took the oath of office as the nation teetered on the brink of dissolution. Seven Southern states had already seceded from the Union. Lincoln appealed to the better angels of our nature, seeking reconciliation despite the sectional rage that threatened to tear the country apart. He repudiated secession as unconstitutional and warned that no state had the right to unilaterally dissolve the Union. Yet he made a delicate promise: he would not interfere with slavery where it already existed, repeating the position he had held during his campaign. He pledged to maintain federal authority and defend federal forts, a commitment that would soon lead to armed confrontation at Fort Sumter in April, just weeks away. His address invoked constitutional authority and moral clarity on union while maintaining pragmatism regarding slavery, a balance that within weeks gave way to the Civil War. Rumors and reports of Confederate attack plans interrupted the proceedings, reflecting the deep national instability of the moment. Lincoln's inaugural address set the tone for his presidency: he would preserve the Constitution, defend federal power, and ultimately confront the question of whether a nation conceived in liberty could endure.
